title: A Lost Suitcase in Istanbul
summary: Layla's suitcase does not arrive in Istanbul, but a kind airport clerk helps her.
body: Layla had planned her first trip to Istanbul for months. She had booked a small hotel near the old bazaar, and she had saved enough money for two weeks of exploring. However, when she arrived at the airport, her suitcase did not appear on the belt. She waited until the hall was almost empty, then went to the lost luggage desk. The clerk, a friendly woman named Selin, explained that the bag had been sent to Ankara by mistake. 'It will be delivered tomorrow morning, so that you can still enjoy your holiday,' she promised. Layla felt worried, because most of her clothes and her camera were inside. Selin lent her a phone charger and wrote down the address of a cheap shop near the hotel. The next day, the suitcase arrived before breakfast, and Layla smiled at the city for the first time.

words.def: a bag you take when travelling
a market with many small shops
a device that fills a battery
said certainly that something will happen

questions.q: Where did Layla plan to spend her holiday?
What was inside the suitcase besides clothes?
When was the suitcase delivered?

title: Omar's First Week at Work
summary: Omar starts a new design job in Toronto and settles into his team during his first week.
body: Omar started a new job at a design company in Toronto on Monday. By Friday, he had already learned the names of everyone on his team. His manager, Grace, told him that questions were always welcome, so that nobody wasted time guessing. At first Omar felt nervous, because the software was new to him, but a colleague named Priya offered to train him during lunch breaks. She had worked at the company for five years and knew every shortcut. Omar also discovered that the office closed early on Fridays, which surprised him pleasantly. On his last morning of the week, he fixed a small problem with the website, and Grace thanked him in front of the team. Although he was still learning, Omar felt that he had made the right choice. He went home tired but happy.

words.def: the person who leads a team
a quicker way to do something
in a nice and happy way
the thing you decide to take

questions.q: Where does Omar work now?
questions.a: At a design company in Toronto.

questions.q: Who trains Omar during lunch breaks?
What did Omar fix on Friday morning?
questions.a: A small problem with the website.

title: Training for the London Marathon
summary: Emma trains for six months and finishes her first London marathon in just over four hours.
body: Emma had never run more than ten kilometres before she decided to enter the London Marathon. Her friends thought she was joking, but she printed a training plan and stuck it on the kitchen wall. For six months she ran before work, even when it rained, so that her body would be ready for the long distance. In January she caught a cold, however, and had to rest for two weeks. Although the break worried her, her coach reminded her that rest is part of training. On race day the streets were crowded with thousands of runners and loud supporters. When Emma finally crossed the finish line after four hours and twelve minutes, her legs shook, but she felt proud. She has already signed up for next year, and this time she wants to run it faster.

words.def: a person who trains sports players
the place where a race ends
put your name on a list

questions.q: How long did Emma train for the race?
What happened to Emma in January?
What is Emma's goal for next year?

title: Kofi's Fruit Stall in Nairobi
summary: Kofi grows his small fruit business in Nairobi and has already repaid half of his loan.
body: Kofi sells fruit from a small stall in the centre of Nairobi. Two years ago he borrowed money from his uncle so that he could buy scales, a table and a roof against the sun. At first he sold only bananas and oranges, but customers kept asking for mangoes, so he added them quickly. He wakes at five every morning to choose the best fruit at the market before the crowd arrives. His prices are written on a piece of card, and he never changes them during the day. Last month he employed his cousin Zola to help on Saturdays, which are the busiest days. Kofi has already paid back half of the loan. If business continues to grow like this, he will open a second stall next year.

words.def: a small open table for selling
took money and will return it
people who buy from a shop
with the most work or people

questions.q: Who lent Kofi money two years ago?
What time does Kofi wake up?
How much of the loan has Kofi paid back?

title: Mei Learns Her Grandmother's Recipe
summary: Mei travels to Busan to learn her grandmother's soup recipe and now cooks it weekly.
body: Mei moved to Seoul for university, but the food there never tasted like home. She missed her grandmother's soup so much that she finally telephoned her and asked for the recipe. Her grandmother laughed and said that the secret could not be written down; it had to be shown. So during the spring holiday, Mei took a train to Busan and spent three days in the old kitchen. She was shown how to wash the rice, when to add the vegetables, and how long the soup must simmer quietly. Her grandmother kept saying, 'Taste it, then taste it again.' On the last evening, Mei cooked the whole meal alone, and her grandmother said it tasted almost right. Mei photographed every step so that she would not forget. Now she cooks the soup for her flatmates every Sunday.

words.def: the steps for cooking a dish
something known only to few people
try a food with the mouth

questions.q: Why did Mei telephone her grandmother?
Where does Mei's grandmother live?
How often does Mei cook the soup now?

title: Marco Moves to a Hilly City
summary: Marco settles into hilly Lisbon, gets stronger, and slowly feels that the city is home.
body: When Marco accepted a job in Lisbon, he had only visited the city once, for a weekend. He found a small flat on a steep street in the old quarter, where laundry hangs between the windows like flags. At first the hills defeated him; after climbing home with heavy shopping bags, he arrived red and breathless. However, within a month his legs had grown stronger, and the stairs no longer frightened him. Marco discovered a tiny cafe at the corner where the owner saves him a table by the window. He has started learning Portuguese in the evenings, although most of his neighbours speak some English. Yesterday an elderly lady from the fourth floor invited him for dinner. Marco says the city felt like a stranger in summer, but now it is starting to feel like home.

words.def: a person you do not know

questions.q: Where did Marco find his flat?
questions.a: On a steep street in the old quarter.

questions.q: What has Marco started learning in the evenings?
Who invited Marco for dinner yesterday?
questions.a: An elderly lady from the fourth floor.

title: Amina Overcomes Her Fear of Water
summary: As an adult in Sydney, Amina takes swimming lessons and slowly beats her fear of water.
body: Amina grew up far from the sea and never learned to swim as a child. When she moved to Sydney, she felt embarrassed at the beach, because all her friends could swim easily. Last summer she finally joined an adult class at a local pool. Her teacher, a patient man named Ken, started with simple breathing exercises at the edge. Amina was terrified during the first lesson, but she was never forced to put her head underwater before she felt ready. Little by little, her confidence grew. By the end of the course she could swim a whole width without stopping. Now she goes to the pool twice a week, and she has promised herself that next year she will try swimming in the ocean. 'If I had started earlier, I would have enjoyed more summers,' she says.

words.def: feeling ashamed in front of people
belief that you can do something
the distance from side to side

questions.q: Where did Amina take swimming lessons?
How did Amina feel at the beach before?
How often does Amina go to the pool now?

title: Khaled Brings an Old Car Back
summary: Khaled spends eight months repairing his grandfather's old car with help from a classic car club.
body: Khaled's grandfather left him an old car that had stood in a garage for fifteen years. Most people told him to sell it for parts, but Khaled had watched his grandfather repair engines as a boy, and the memories were worth more than money. Every weekend he removed one broken piece and studied how a new one should be fitted. He found videos online that explained each step clearly, and he joined a club for classic cars in his city. Members often visited his garage so that they could share tools and advice. After eight months, the engine started on the second try, and the whole street heard the loud, happy noise. Khaled has driven the car twice now, slowly and carefully. 'If my grandfather could see it, he would laugh,' he says.

words.def: a building where cars are kept
helpful ideas about what to do
things you remember from the past

questions.q: How long had the car stood in the garage?
What did Khaled find online?
How many times has Khaled driven the car?

title: Yuki Volunteers at the Library
summary: After losing her job, Yuki volunteers at a library and gains confidence and a possible position.
body: After Yuki lost her job at a bookshop, she spent several dull weeks searching online. Her neighbour, who works at a public library, suggested that she volunteer there twice a week while she looked for something new. At first Yuki only shelved books and repaired torn covers, but slowly she was given more interesting tasks. She now runs a small reading corner for children on Saturday mornings, where they listen to stories and draw pictures. The children have already chosen her as their favourite storyteller, although she still reads in a shy voice. The library has also become useful in another way: last month the manager mentioned a part-time position in the events team, and Yuki applied the same day. Whatever happens with the job, she says the voluntary work has given her confidence and a reason to leave the house.

words.def: working only some hours a week

questions.q: Why did Yuki start volunteering?
What does Yuki do on Saturday mornings?
questions.a: She runs a reading corner for children.

questions.q: What did the library manager mention last month?
questions.a: A part-time position in the events team.

title: Fatou's Battle with Night Shifts
summary: Nurse Fatou improves her daytime sleep with simple new habits and shares them with her sister.
body: Fatou is a nurse who has worked night shifts for three years. Sleeping during the day was almost impossible at first, because sunlight and street noise kept waking her. She tried many solutions: thick curtains, earplugs, even a fan for white noise. Nothing helped completely until she made one simple change. Now she turns off her phone an hour before bed and drinks warm milk instead of coffee. Her sleep has improved so much that she no longer feels tired at work, and her concentration is better with patients. Fatou also told her sister, who works in a bakery before dawn, about the routine, and it helped her too. Although night work will never feel natural, Fatou believes that good habits can protect your health. 'Your body needs rules, even at strange hours,' she often says.

words.def: small things put in ears to block noise
things you do the same way often
things you do again and again

questions.q: How long has Fatou worked night shifts?
What does Fatou drink before bed?
Who else tried Fatou's routine?

title: Ivan's Small Team, Big Dream
summary: Ivan's village football team trains hard all winter and beats the top team in spring.
body: Ivan has played football for a village team since he was seven. Last season the team finished last, and several players wanted to quit, but the coach refused to give up. He asked everyone to meet twice a week, even in winter, so that they would be ready for the next season. Training was hard: running up the hill behind the field, passing drills in the cold, and matches against much bigger clubs. However, the players grew closer, and their passing became faster and sharper. In the spring they beat the top team 2-1, and the whole village celebrated in the square. Although they finished in the middle of the table, Ivan feels proud. 'If we keep training like this, one day we will win the cup,' he told the local newspaper.

words.def: stop doing a job or activity
showed joy about a good event
the months when games are played

questions.q: How often did the team meet in winter?
What was the result against the top team?
Who did Ivan speak to?

title: Priya Wins the Science Fair
summary: Priya builds a solar oven for her science project, fixes her failures, and wins first prize.
body: For months Priya had wanted to build something useful for her science project. She read that a box, foil and glass could cook food using only sunlight, so she decided to build a solar oven. Her first attempt failed badly: the box lost heat, and the rice stayed hard. Instead of quitting, she covered the inside with black paper and added a second glass lid to trap the warmth. On the day of the science fair, she melted cheese on bread in front of the judges, and the smell filled the hall. She won first prize, but the best moment came later. A teacher from another school asked whether she could copy the design for her class. Priya has already uploaded simple instructions online so that anyone can build one for free.

words.def: a plan showing how something works
steps that tell you what to do

questions.q: What did Priya build for her project?
What went wrong with her first attempt?
Where has Priya uploaded instructions?

title: Tom Learns to Manage Money
summary: Tom changes his spending habits with an app and three rules, then saves for a trip to Lisbon.
body: Tom always spent his salary in the first two weeks, then borrowed small amounts from friends until payday. When he missed a rent payment last spring, he knew the system had to change. He downloaded an app that records every purchase and showed him where the money disappeared: taxi rides, snack machines and late-night shopping. Tom made three rules for himself. He now takes a fixed amount of cash out each Monday, he cooks dinner four times a week, and he moves a little money into savings before he can touch it. After six months he has saved enough for a short trip to Lisbon, something he had wanted for years. His friends laugh, but they have also started asking for advice. 'If you can see where it goes, you can stop it,' Tom says.

words.def: money you get for your job
money you keep for the future
went away so you could not see it
helpful ideas about what to do

questions.q: What did Tom download?
questions.a: An app that records every purchase.

questions.q: How many times a week does Tom cook dinner?
What has Tom saved enough for?

title: Elena's First Exhibition
summary: Elena shows her paintings publicly for the first time in a Barcelona gallery and sells two.
body: Elena had painted in her tiny flat for ten years without showing her work to anyone. Her sister secretly sent photos of three paintings to a small gallery in Barcelona, and to everyone's surprise, the owner offered her a wall for September. Preparing the exhibition took weeks: Elena chose twelve pieces, framed them and wrote a short text about each one. The night before the opening she hardly slept. However, the opening was warm and friendly, and visitors kept asking about her colours and her unusual angles. A local magazine interviewed her, and a cafe owner bought two paintings for his dining room. Elena has not sold many more since then, but something has changed. 'I used to paint for the wall,' she says. 'Now I paint for people.'

words.def: a place where art is shown
a public show of art or objects
the first public day of an event
people who come to see a place
the directions you view something from

title: Ken Builds an App for Buses
summary: Ken creates a free bus-tracking app for his city that thousands of people quickly download.
body: Ken lives in a busy city where he waits for buses every morning. The timetable at the stop is often wrong, and once he was late for an important exam. That evening he decided to act. Ken had studied programming at college, so he began to build a small app that shows where each bus really is, using public data from the transport company. Friends tested early versions and reported problems, which he fixed one by one. Six months later the app was offered free in the local store, and thousands of people downloaded it in the first week. The transport company was so impressed that it now shares live information directly with Ken's app. Although he works on it in his free time, Ken says the project has taught him more than any course.

words.def: a list of times and events
different forms of the same product
gives part of something to others

questions.q: What made Ken late once?
What does the app show?

title: Zola's Community Garden
summary: Zola turns a rubbish-filled space behind her flats into a garden that unites her neighbours.
body: The empty space behind Zola's block of flats was full of rubbish and old tyres. One Saturday she put on gloves, called a few neighbours, and started clearing it. What began as a clean-up became a community garden. Families now grow tomatoes, spinach and herbs in boxes made from recycled wood, and a rain tank waters them when the weather is dry. The children have their own small plot, where they have planted sunflowers and beans. Zola says the vegetables taste better than anything from the supermarket, but the greatest change is social. People who never greeted each other now share tools, seeds and recipes. The city council has noticed the project and offered two more empty spaces. 'If everyone gave one hour a week, we could feed the whole street,' Zola laughs.

words.def: used again in a new form
the group that runs a city
small things that grow into plants

questions.q: What did the space behind the flats contain?
Who has planted sunflowers and beans?
What has the city council offered?

title: Sofia Finds a Language Partner
summary: Sofia improves her Greek through a free language exchange with a taxi driver in Athens.
body: Sofia moved to Athens for work, but after a year she still could not hold a real conversation in Greek. Classes helped her grammar, yet she froze whenever someone spoke at normal speed. Then a colleague suggested a language exchange: she would teach English for an hour and practise Greek for an hour, with no money involved. Her partner, Nikos, was a taxi driver who wanted English for tourists. They met twice a week in a quiet cafe near the harbour. At first they laughed a lot at their mistakes, which made learning less frightening. After three months, Sofia ordered food, argued politely about football and even understood a radio phone-in. She has made mistakes since then, of course, but now she starts conversations instead of waiting. 'A language lives in people, not in books,' she says.

words.def: talk between two or more people
giving one thing and getting another
in a kind and respectful way
things done in the wrong way

questions.q: What did Sofia teach Nikos?
Where did they meet?
questions.a: In a quiet cafe near the harbour.

questions.q: When could Sofia order food in Greek?

title: Jack and the Noisy Flat
summary: Jack solves flatmate conflict in Manchester by holding a short meeting and writing house rules.
body: Jack shared a flat in Manchester with two students whose idea of cleaning was very different from his. Dishes stayed in the sink for days, and nobody ever bought milk. At first Jack said nothing, because he did not want an argument. However, the problem grew, and one evening he almost moved out. Instead, he called a short flat meeting and wrote three house rules on paper: everyone washes their own dishes, shopping money is shared, and loud music ends at eleven. The others agreed surprisingly easily. Nothing is perfect, and the sink is not always shining, but the atmosphere at home is much better. Jack has learned that silence often makes problems bigger. 'If you speak early and kindly, most people listen,' he tells friends who now face the same trouble.

words.def: the basin where you wash dishes
in a friendly and gentle way

questions.q: With whom did Jack share a flat?

title: Hana's Night Train Adventure
summary: Hana takes a cheaper night train to Vienna, makes friends, and now prefers travelling by rail.
body: Hana wanted to visit Vienna, but flights were expensive during the holiday season, so she booked a seat on the night train instead. The idea of sleeping while the country passed outside seemed romantic, and it was cheaper than a hotel too. Reality was less peaceful: the train stopped twice, doors slammed, and at midnight a family with a small baby joined her compartment. However, at sunrise the fields turned gold, and hot coffee appeared from the dining car. By the time the train reached Vienna, Hana had made two new friends and plans to meet again. She arrived at the hotel earlier than expected, left her bag there, and walked straight to the old centre. Since that trip, she has chosen the train whenever she can.

words.def: arranged a place before you go
a small room on a train
the time when the sun comes up

questions.q: Why did Hana take the night train?
What joined her compartment at midnight?
questions.a: A family with a small baby.

questions.q: Where did Hana leave her bag?

title: Leo and the Castle Guide
summary: Leo becomes a castle guide in Edinburgh, studies every evening, and eventually trains new guides.
body: Leo took a summer job as a guide at an old castle in Edinburgh. On his first day he memorised a page of dates and facts, but visitors asked questions that the page never answered. One old lady wanted to know what the soldiers ate; a boy asked why the walls were so thick. Leo started reading in the castle library every evening so that he could give better answers. Slowly his tours changed: instead of reciting numbers, he told stories about the people who had lived there, from cooks to kings. Children began to listen, and adults stayed after the tour with more questions. Leo has now worked there for two years and trains new guides himself. 'Walls do not remember anything,' he tells them. 'People remember, so we must tell their stories.'

words.def: a large old stone building for kings
wide from one side to the other

questions.q: Where did Leo take a summer job?
questions.a: At an old castle in Edinburgh.

questions.q: Where did Leo read every evening?
How long has Leo worked there?

title: Rania and the Potter's Wheel
summary: Rania learns pottery in Marrakesh from a patient master over several weekends.
body: On a school trip to Marrakesh, Rania watched an old potter shape clay into a perfect bowl in under a minute. She asked if she could try, and the man laughed kindly and moved aside. Her first pot collapsed immediately; her second looked like a broken cup. Rania returned every weekend for a month, paying small fees from her pocket money. The potter, whose family has made tiles for four generations, never let her give up. He corrected her hands gently and repeated the same words: patience, water, patience. By the end of the month she produced four honest bowls, imperfect but strong. Her family now eats from them every evening. Rania has decided to learn the family trade seriously, and the potter says that if she continues, her hands will one day remember everything.

words.def: a person who makes clay pots
soft wet earth used for pots
groups of people born around the same time

questions.q: Where did Rania first see the potter?
questions.a: On a school trip to Marrakesh.

questions.q: How did the potter help her?
How many bowls did Rania produce?

title: Daniel Joins the Chess Club
summary: Daniel leaves online chess for a real club, fixes one weakness, and draws against the top member.
body: Daniel had played chess online for years, always against strangers, and he was quite good. When a colleague invited him to a real chess club, however, he discovered a different world. Online, games are fast and faces are hidden; at the club, an opponent sits across the table, watches your eyes and thinks for long minutes. Daniel lost his first five games badly and nearly gave up. Instead, he asked the club's oldest member, a retired teacher named Peter, for help. Peter studied three of Daniel's games and showed him one simple weakness: he always attacked too early. Daniel practised defence for two months. Last Thursday he drew against Peter himself, and half the club applauded. He has stopped playing online almost completely now.

words.def: no longer working because of age
the part where someone is not strong
finished a game with equal scores
hit hands together to show praise

questions.q: Who invited Daniel to the chess club?
What was Daniel's weakness?
What did Daniel do last Thursday?

title: Sami's Sunday Beach Clean-Up
summary: Sami's simple online message brings thirty volunteers to clean an Alexandria beach, and the habit spreads.
body: Sami runs a small cafe near the beach in Alexandria. Every Monday morning, plastic bags and bottles covered the sand, left by weekend visitors. Complaining changed nothing, so one Sunday he posted a simple message online: gloves and bags provided, meet at eight, breakfast afterwards for volunteers. He expected four or five friends. Instead, thirty people appeared, including a family visiting from Cairo. The group filled forty large bags in two hours, and the children turned the work into a treasure hunt for bottle caps. The cafe now hosts the clean-up monthly, and a local school has adopted the beach for its projects. The sea looks different after each Sunday, Sami says, but the real result is invisible: a community that feels responsible for its own shore. 'People protect what they touch,' he believes.

words.def: a game of looking for hidden things
invites people and organises an event
chose to take care of something
having the duty to care for something

questions.q: Who appeared to help Sami?
questions.a: Thirty people, including a family from Cairo.

questions.q: How many bags did the group fill?
How often is the clean-up held?

title: Emma's Surprise at the Airport
summary: Emma meets an old university friend by chance at Sydney airport during a flight delay.
body: Emma was waiting at Sydney airport for a long flight home to London when she heard a familiar laugh behind her. She turned around and saw her old university friend Grace, whom she had not met for eight years. Grace had been working in Australia for six months and was flying home for her sister's wedding. They had two hours before their flights, so they found a quiet corner, bought terrible airport coffee and talked without stopping. Emma had recently changed jobs, and Grace had travelled through Asia, but it felt as if no time had passed at all. They exchanged numbers, promised to meet in London, and took photos together. On the plane, Emma realised that the delay she had complained about had given her something far better than punctuality: an old friendship, fresh and alive again.

words.def: known because you have seen it before

questions.q: Where did Emma meet Grace?
How long had the friends not met?
Why was Grace flying home?

title: Call: Booking a Hotel Room
summary: A phone dialogue in which a guest books a double room with a sea view by email confirmation.
body: A: Good morning, Sunset Hotel, how can I help you? B: Hello, I would like to book a double room for three nights from the twelfth of July. A: Certainly. Would you like a room with a sea view or a garden view? B: The sea view, please, if it is not too expensive. A: It is forty dollars more per night, but breakfast is included. B: That sounds fair. Is there parking at the hotel? A: Yes, parking is free for guests, and we also have a small pool. B: Perfect. Could you send me a confirmation by email? A: Of course. Your booking is confirmed, and the email will arrive within the hour.

words.def: what you can see from a window
people who stay at a hotel
an arrangement to keep a room
a message that proves the arrangement

questions.q: How many nights does the caller want?
How much more does the sea view cost?
When will the confirmation email arrive?

title: Visit to the Doctor
summary: A doctor examines a patient with a sore throat and fever and advises rest, water and medicine.
body: A: Good afternoon. What seems to be the problem today? B: I have had a sore throat and a headache for three days, and last night I started coughing. A: Do you have a fever? B: Slightly, I think. My temperature was 38 degrees this morning. A: Your throat is red, but it does not look serious. It is probably a common virus, so antibiotics will not help. B: What should I do at home? A: Rest, drink plenty of water, and take this medicine for the pain. If you are not better after five days, come back. B: Should I stay home from work? A: Yes, for at least two days. You need rest more than anything.

words.def: a tiny thing that causes illness
pushing air out of the throat loudly

questions.q: How long has the patient felt ill?
What was the patient's temperature this morning?
How long should the patient stay home from work?

title: Job Interview Questions
summary: An interviewer asks a candidate about experience, strengths and weaknesses during a calm job interview.
body: A: Thank you for coming today. Tell me a little about your experience. B: I have worked as a shop assistant for three years, and last year I became responsible for ordering stock. A: Why do you want to change jobs? B: I would like more challenge and the chance to work with customers in a bigger company. A: What would you say is your greatest strength? B: I stay calm when things get busy, and I solve problems quickly. A: When could you start, if we offered you the position? B: I would need one month to finish my current projects. A: That is fine. We will contact you by Friday. B: Thank you very much for your time.

words.def: knowledge gained by doing a job
the goods a shop keeps for sale

questions.q: How long has the candidate worked as a shop assistant?
What is the candidate's greatest strength?
questions.a: Staying calm and solving problems quickly.

questions.q: When will the company contact the candidate?

title: Returning Shoes to the Shop
summary: A shop assistant helps a customer whose running shoes hurt, suggesting a wider model instead of a refund.
body: A: Good morning. How can I help you? B: I bought these running shoes here last week, but they hurt my feet when I walk. A: I see. Do you have the receipt with you? B: Yes, here it is. They were forty-five pounds. A: Would you like to exchange them for a different size, or would you prefer a refund? B: Could I try a larger size first? A: Of course. What size do you normally wear? B: Size nine, but these feel tight on the sides. A: The problem might be the shape, not the size. These are narrow. I can show you a wider model in the same price range.

words.def: money given back to a buyer
not wide; small from side to side
the outer form of a thing

questions.q: When did the customer buy the shoes?
How much did the shoes cost?
What does the assistant suggest?
questions.a: A wider model in the same price range.

title: Asking for Directions Downtown
summary: A helpful stranger gives a tourist walking and bus directions to the National Museum.
body: A: Excuse me, could you help me? I am looking for the National Museum. B: Of course. It is about fifteen minutes on foot. Go straight along this street and turn left at the fountain. A: Left at the fountain. Is it far from there? B: No, you will see the museum on your right, opposite a small park. A: Is there a bus, in case it rains? B: Yes, the number twelve stops directly in front of it, and buses run every ten minutes. A: That is good to know. Is the museum open today? B: It is open until six, but the special exhibition closes at four, I believe. A: Thank you so much. You have been very helpful. B: No problem. Enjoy your visit, and mind the steps near the fountain.

words.def: a structure that sends water up
in a straight and exact way
a public show of art or objects

questions.q: How far is the museum on foot?
Which bus goes to the museum?
When does the special exhibition close?

title: Joining the Local Library
summary: A librarian explains membership, borrowing limits, renewals and the free study room to a newcomer.
body: A: Hello, I have just moved to this area. I would like to join the library. B: Welcome. You will need to fill in a short form and show a document with your address. A: Does a recent electricity bill work? B: Yes, that is fine. Membership is free for residents, and you can borrow up to eight books at a time. A: How long can I keep them? B: For three weeks, and you can renew them twice online if nobody has reserved them. A: What about audiobooks and films? B: We have both, and they follow the same rules. There is also a free study room on the second floor. A: This is perfect. I study in the evenings, so the quiet room will be very useful. B: Then fill in this form, and your card will be ready in five minutes.

title: The Sweet Food That Never Spoils
summary: Info item explaining why honey almost never spoils, how bees make it, and its old medical uses.
body: Honey is one of the few foods that almost never spoils. Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient tombs that were still safe to eat after thousands of years. The reason is chemistry: honey contains very little water, and its natural acidity makes life difficult for bacteria. Bees make honey from the nectar of flowers, and a single worker bee produces only about a twelfth of a teaspoon in her whole life. For this reason, a jar of honey represents the work of millions of flowers and thousands of bees. If honey becomes cloudy or solid in the jar, it has not gone bad; warming it gently returns it to liquid. Honey has also been used for centuries to dress wounds, because it keeps the skin clean and moist.

title: How Water Travels Around Earth
summary: Info item describing the water cycle, from evaporation and clouds to rain, rivers and the sea.
body: The water cycle describes how the same water moves around our planet again and again. The sun heats rivers, lakes and oceans, and water rises into the air as invisible vapour. High above the ground, the vapour cools and forms tiny drops, which gather together as clouds. When the drops become heavy enough, they fall back to Earth as rain or snow. Some of this water sinks into the soil and feeds plants and underground streams; the rest flows back to the sea. The cycle has no beginning and no end, and it has continued for billions of years. The water you drink today may once have fallen on a forest, frozen on a mountain, or even passed through a dinosaur. Water is never created or destroyed; it simply keeps moving.

title: Coral Reefs: Cities Under the Sea
summary: Info item about coral reefs, the tiny polyps that build them, their value and the threats they face.
body: Coral reefs are sometimes called the rainforests of the sea, because they are home to an enormous variety of life. Although reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, about a quarter of all known sea species spend part of their lives there. A reef is built by tiny animals called polyps, which produce a hard, stone-like material around themselves. The bright colours actually come from microscopic plants that live inside the polyps and provide them with food. Reefs protect coastlines from storms, support fishing communities and attract tourists from around the world. However, reefs grow extremely slowly, often less than a centimetre a year, so damage can take decades to repair. Scientists warn that warmer water is the greatest danger, and many countries have now created protected areas to help reefs recover.

title: Public Libraries Are Changing
summary: Info item about how modern public libraries lend more than books and serve whole communities.
body: A public library is one of the few places where anyone can spend hours without paying anything. Traditionally, libraries were quiet rooms full of books, and visitors were told to keep silent. Today, however, many libraries have become lively centres of the community. People borrow not only books but also music, films and sometimes tools or kitchen equipment. Free internet, study rooms and language classes attract students and job seekers, while children enjoy story hours and small events. Librarians have become guides to information: they help people find reliable answers, fill in official forms and use new technology. Although fewer paper books are borrowed than in the past, studies show that visits to libraries have stayed high. A good library proves that a city can offer knowledge, shelter and help without asking for money in return.

title: Why Cities Love the Bicycle
summary: Info item on how bicycles save time, cut pollution, improve health and are supported by modern cities.
body: The bicycle was invented in the nineteenth century, and it remains one of the cleverest machines ever built. It turns the energy of your legs into smooth movement with very little waste, and it needs no fuel except food. In many modern cities, bicycles have become a serious answer to traffic and pollution. Riding a bike is often faster than driving in the centre, because bicycles can pass queues of cars and park almost anywhere. Doctors also point out that regular cycling strengthens the heart and lowers stress. Several cities have therefore built wide cycle lanes, and some have created bike-sharing systems where anyone can rent a bicycle with a phone. Although cycling in heavy traffic feels dangerous at first, most riders gain confidence quickly, and studies show that cycling is safer than many people believe.

title: The World's Largest Hot Desert
summary: Info item about the Sahara: its size, terrain, extreme temperatures and surprising green past.
body: The Sahara, in North Africa, is the largest hot desert in the world. It covers an area almost as large as the whole of the United States, and eleven countries share its territory. People often imagine endless sand, but only about a quarter of the Sahara is covered by dunes; the rest is rocky plateaus, mountains and gravel plains. Temperatures can rise above fifty degrees in summer, yet winter nights can fall below freezing. Rain is rare, and some regions receive none for years, so plants and animals survive with special tricks. Camels store fat rather than water, and desert foxes hunt at night when the sand is cooler. Surprisingly, the Sahara was not always dry: thousands of years ago, rock paintings show that lakes, fish and elephants existed there.

title: The Amazing World of Languages
summary: Info item on world languages: their number, borrowed words, dying languages and the value of learning one.
body: Linguists believe that around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, although almost half of them may disappear within this century. The most widely spoken language by native speakers is Mandarin Chinese, while English is the most studied second language. Languages borrow from each other constantly: English has taken thousands of words, including 'tea' from Chinese and 'sugar' from Arabic. Every two weeks, according to researchers, the last speaker of some language dies, and with that voice a whole way of seeing the world disappears. Languages are more than tools, however; they carry stories, humour and history. Learning even one foreign language trains memory, sharpens attention and opens a door to another culture.

title: Rainforests: The Green Engine

body: Tropical rainforests grow near the equator, where it is hot and rains almost every day. Although they cover only a small part of the Earth's land, they contain more than half of all plant and animal species. A single hectare of rainforest can hold more kinds of trees than all of Europe. The forest works like a giant engine: trees pull water from the soil and release it into the air, creating the clouds that water distant farms. Rainforests also store enormous amounts of carbon, which helps to slow climate change. Unfortunately, large areas are still cut down for farming and timber, and once the soil loses its roots, it quickly becomes poor and dry. Many medicines were first discovered in rainforest plants, and scientists believe countless more remain unknown to us.

title: Three Hearts and Blue Blood
summary: Info item on the octopus: its three hearts, blue blood, boneless escape skills and clever behaviour.
body: The octopus is one of the strangest animals in the ocean. It has three hearts, blue blood and no bones in its whole body except a hard beak in its mouth. Because it has no skeleton, an octopus can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak, so even a heavy individual can escape through a hole the size of a coin. Octopuses are also famously intelligent: they open jars, recognise individual people and can remember solutions to problems. If danger approaches, many species change colour and texture in less than a second to match their surroundings. Female octopuses usually die soon after their eggs hatch, but before that they guard them carefully for weeks. Scientists study octopuses closely, because their clever minds developed completely separately from ours, along a very different path of evolution.

title: The Great Wall of China
summary: Info item on the Great Wall's long construction, true length, smoke signals and its status as a myth-buster.
body: The Great Wall of China is the longest structure ever built by humans. It was not constructed at one time or by one ruler: several states began building defensive walls more than two thousand years ago, and these were later joined together and extended, mainly during the Ming dynasty, between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries. All the branches together stretch for more than twenty thousand kilometres, crossing mountains, deserts and grasslands. Contrary to a popular story, the wall cannot be seen from the moon with the naked eye, although astronauts can photograph parts of it from low orbit. The wall was guarded by soldiers who used smoke signals to warn of attacks: one smoke column meant about a hundred enemies. Today millions of tourists visit restored sections near Beijing every year.

title: What Happens While You Sleep
summary: Info item on sleep stages, deep and REM sleep, how much adults need and what improves sleep quality.
body: Sleep is not one long pause; it is a cycle of different stages that repeats several times each night. In deep sleep, the body repairs muscles, strengthens the immune system and releases growth hormone, which is why teenagers need more sleep than adults. In another stage, called REM sleep, the brain becomes almost as active as when you are awake, and most dreams happen. During this stage, the brain seems to organise memories and connect new information with old knowledge. Adults usually need between seven and nine hours, but quality matters as much as quantity. A cool, dark and quiet room improves sleep, while screens, coffee and heavy meals late at night make it worse. People who regularly sleep too little find it harder to concentrate, remember and control their emotions.

title: The Story of Olive Oil
summary: Info item on olive oil's ancient history, traditional uses, how it is made and its health value.
body: Olives have been grown around the Mediterranean for more than six thousand years, and olive oil was one of the first traded goods in the ancient world. It was used for cooking, for light in clay lamps, for skin care and even as a prize for winners of early sports games. Producing oil is simple in principle: ripe olives are crushed into a paste, which is pressed so that the golden liquid runs out. Extra virgin olive oil, the highest quality, comes only from the first pressing and has a fresh, slightly fruity taste. Olive trees are remarkably tough: they survive poor soil and little rain, and some trees alive today were planted centuries ago. Doctors consider olive oil a healthy fat, especially for the heart.

title: Birds That Swim Instead of Fly

On land their walk looks clumsy, yet the same birds can dive hundreds of metres deep and hold their breath for many minutes. Penguins live almost entirely in the southern half of the world, from the cold ice of Antarctica to warm beaches near the equator; the famous emperor penguin is the largest species, and the little penguin of Australia and New Zealand is the smallest. A remarkable example of parenting is shown by emperor penguins: the male keeps the single egg warm on his feet through the freezing winter while the female feeds at sea. Penguins are protected by thick feathers and a layer of fat.

title: A Short History of Money
summary: Info item tracing money from barter to the first coins in Lydia, paper money in China and digital money.
body: Before money existed, people exchanged goods directly: a farmer might swap grain for shoes or for a pot. This system, called barter, works badly, however, because both sides must want exactly what the other offers. Coins solved the problem. The first known coins were made about two thousand seven hundred years ago in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, from a naturally occurring mixture of gold and silver. Paper money appeared much later, in China, where merchants grew tired of carrying heavy coins. Today most money is not physical at all; it is simply numbers moved between computers. Yet the basic idea has never changed: money is a shared agreement that makes exchange easier, so that a baker can sell bread today and trust that the value will still count tomorrow.

title: Essay: Online or Classroom?
summary: Write a short opinion essay: is online learning better than classroom learning?
body: In my opinion, online learning and classroom learning are useful in different situations, and neither is better for everyone. Online courses have clear advantages. Students can study at any hour, repeat difficult parts as often as necessary and save the time and money spent travelling. For people with jobs or small children, this flexibility is essential. However, classrooms offer something that screens cannot copy so easily. Learners speak with real people, make friends and practise conversation without long silences, and a good teacher notices immediately when someone is confused. In my experience, online lessons suit independent students who already have good study habits, while beginners and social learners progress faster in a classroom. Ideally, the two should be combined: knowledge can be gained online, but skills are practised together. That balance seems the best solution.

title: Forum: Advice for New Students
summary: Write a forum post giving advice to a new student who is moving to your town.
body: Welcome to our town! I moved here two years ago, and I remember how confusing the first month felt, so here is my advice. First, find a flat early, because good rooms disappear quickly in September. The areas near the river are cheaper, and buses run all night. Second, buy a monthly travel card as soon as you arrive; it pays for itself in a week. Third, do not buy every book on the reading list. The library has copies of almost everything, and second-hand shops sell older editions for very little. Finally, join at least one club, even if it sounds strange. I met my best friends at the hiking club, and it costs nothing. Good luck, and feel free to ask more questions below. Posted by Tom B.
